summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over an IPv4 domain, and how to form IPv6 link-local addresses, without explicit tunnels. It treats an IPv4 multicast network as a virtual link, and defines the link-layer address option used in neighbor discovery messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a way to run IPv6 over an IPv4 network that has multicast. The IPv4 multicast area acts as the local link: each machine wraps its IPv6 packets in IPv4 packets, uses its IPv4 address to build its own IPv6 link-local address, and discovers neighbours over IPv4 multicast.

questions: how does ipv6 over ipv4 multicast work
what is the default mtu for 6over4
how is a 6over4 link-local address formed
subtitle: Carries IPv6 packets across an IPv4 network by treating the IPv4 multicast domain as a virtual local link.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 host on a physical link with no IPv6 router has no way to use IPv6, unless the site configures tunnels or IPv4-compatible addresses on every host.
tldr.mechanism: The mechanism puts IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets with protocol type 41 and uses the IPv4 multicast domain as a virtual local link. Each host forms a link-local address from FE80::/64 and its IPv4 address, and Neighbor Discovery runs over IPv4 multicast.
tldr.outcome: Such a host becomes a fully functional IPv6 host with no manual tunnel configuration. The default IPv6 MTU over an IPv4 domain is 1480 octets, and the IPv4 do-not-fragment bit must not be set.

today: RFC 2529 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What an IPv4 Domain Means Here
sections.content:
An IPv4 domain, as this document uses the term, is a fully interconnected set of IPv4 subnets, within the same local multicast scope, on which there are at least two IPv6 nodes conforming to this specification. The domain could form part of the globally unique IPv4 address space, or it could form part of a private IPv4 network.

The motivation is to allow isolated IPv6 hosts, located on a physical link that has no directly connected IPv6 router, to become fully functional IPv6 hosts by using an IPv4 domain as their virtual local link. At least one IPv6 router using the same method must be connected to the same IPv4 domain if IPv6 routing to other links is required.

IPv6 hosts connected this way do not require IPv4-compatible addresses or configured tunnels, so IPv6 gains independence from the underlying links and can step over many hops of IPv4 subnets. The mechanism is known formally as IPv6 over IPv4, or 6over4, and colloquially as virtual Ethernet. The document also specifies the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in the Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages, when those messages are transmitted on an IPv4 multicast domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv4 multicast area acts as the local link: every machine on the site can reach it. This document describes how to send IPv6 packets over that area and how the machines on it find each other.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit and Time to Live
sections.content:
The default MTU size for IPv6 packets on an IPv4 domain is 1480 octets. This size may be varied by a Router Advertisement containing an MTU option that specifies a different MTU, or by manual configuration of each node.

If the IPv6 MTU size proves to be too large for some intermediate IPv4 subnet, IPv4 fragmentation will ensue. While undesirable, this is not disastrous. However, the IPv4 do-not-fragment bit MUST NOT be set in the encapsulating IPv4 header.

The Time to Live field SHOULD be set to a low value, to prevent such packets accidentally leaking from the IPv4 domain. This MUST be a configurable parameter, with a recommended default of 8.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 packets are limited to 1480 bytes by default here. The TTL is kept low, so a packet that escapes the domain is dropped before it travels far.

sections.title: The Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are transmitted in IPv4 packets with an IPv4 protocol type of 41, the same as has been assigned in RFC 1933 for IPv6 packets that are tunneled inside of IPv4 frames. The IPv4 header contains the destination and source IPv4 addresses. The IPv4 packet body contains the IPv6 header followed immediately by the payload.

If there are IPv4 options, padding SHOULD be added to the IPv4 header such that the IPv6 header starts on a boundary that is a 32-bit offset from the end of the data link header.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 packet is carried unchanged inside an ordinary IPv4 packet, marked with protocol number 41. Nothing in the IPv6 packet itself is altered.

sections.title: Forming the Link-Local Address
sections.content:
The interface identifier of an IPv4 interface is the 32-bit IPv4 address of that interface, with the octets in the same order in which they would appear in the header of an IPv4 packet, padded at the left with zeros to a total of 64 bits. The universal/local bit is zero, indicating that the interface identifier is not globally unique. When the host has more than one IPv4 address in use on the physical interface concerned, an administrative choice of one of these IPv4 addresses is made.

An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of an IPv4 interface MUST have a length of 64 bits, except for a special case mentioned in Section 7. The IPv6 link-local address for an IPv4 virtual interface is formed by appending that interface identifier to the prefix FE80::/64, so the address is FE80:: followed by 32 zero bits and the IPv4 address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each machine builds its own IPv6 link-local address out of its IPv4 address: the fixed prefix FE80::, then zeros, then the IPv4 address itself. The result is unique within the domain but is not a global address.

sections.title: Mapping IPv6 Addresses to IPv4 Link-Layer Addresses
sections.content:
The procedure for mapping IPv6 addresses into IPv4 virtual link-layer addresses is described in RFC 2461. The Source/Target Link-layer Address option has the following form when the link layer is IPv4. Since the length field is in units of 8 bytes, the value is 1.

The Type field is 1 for a source link-layer address and 2 for a target link-layer address. The Length field is 1, in units of 8 octets. The IPv4 Address field holds the 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order. This is the address the interface currently responds to, and may be different from the interface identifier used for stateless autoconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbour Discovery messages need to carry the hardware-level address of a machine. On this virtual link, that is simply its IPv4 address, packed into a standard option with a type of 1 or 2.

sections.title: Mapping Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
IPv4 multicast MUST be available. An IPv6 packet with a multicast destination address MUST be transmitted to the IPv4 multicast address of Organization-Local Scope using the mapping below. These IPv4 multicast addresses SHOULD be taken from the block 239.192.0.0/16, a sub-block of the Organization-Local Scope address block, or, if all of those are not available, from the expansion blocks defined in RFC 2365. When they are formed using the expansion blocks, they use only a /16 sized block.

The last two bytes of the IPv6 multicast address become the last two bytes of the IPv4 multicast address, and the OLS byte comes from the configured Organization-Local Scope address block, where it SHOULD be 192. No new IANA registration procedures are required for this mapping. Appendix A lists the multicast groups that must be joined to support Neighbor Discovery: 239.OLS.0.1 for all nodes, 239.OLS.0.2 for all routers, and 239.OLS.Y.Z for the solicited-node group, where W.X.Y.Z is the IPv4 address used to form the IPv6 address and the IPv6 solicited-node multicast address is FF02::1:255.X.Y.Z.
sections.plainLanguage: Group traffic also has to be translated. The last two bytes of the IPv6 group address are kept, the rest of the IPv4 group address is a fixed local block, and three fixed groups reach all nodes, all routers and the solicited-node group.

sections.title: Scaling and Transition
sections.content:
The multicast mechanism described in Section 6 appears to have essentially the same scaling properties as native IPv6 over most media, except for the slight reduction in MTU size, which slightly reduces bulk throughput. On an ATM network, where IPv4 multicast relies on relatively complex mechanisms, IPv6 over IPv4 over ATM is expected to perform less well than native IPv6 over ATM.

The mechanism is intended to take its place in the range of options available for transition from IPv4 to IPv6. It allows a site to run both IPv4 and IPv6 in coexistence, without configuring IPv6 hosts with IPv4-compatible addresses or tunnels. The interfaces of the IPv6 router and hosts will need to be enabled in 6over4 mode.

A site may start its transition by configuring one IPv6 router to support 6over4 on an interface connected to the site's IPv4 domain, and another IPv6 format on an interface connected to the IPv6 Internet. Any enabled 6over4 hosts in the IPv4 domain can then communicate both with the router and with the IPv6 Internet, without manual configuration of a tunnel and without the need for an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address.

During transition, routers may need to advertise at least two IPv6 prefixes, one for the native LAN and one for 6over4, and the latter MUST be unique within its scope. When a router handles both native LAN and 6over4 on the same physical interface, link-local addresses with the prefix FE80::/64 are used in both cases, and the prefix length for these link-local addresses MUST then be 128 so that the two cases can be distinguished. As the site installs additional IPv6 routers, 6over4 hosts that become physically adjacent to IPv6 routers can be changed to run as native IPv6 hosts, with the only impact on IPv6 applications being a slight increase in MTU size. Dual homing hosts in both native LAN and 6over4 mode might be convenient at some stage, but is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is a way to move a site from IPv4 to IPv6 gradually. One router speaks both, the machines on the old network keep working, and each machine can later be switched to native IPv6 with no change to the applications.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors should be aware that in addition to possible attacks against IPv6, security attacks against IPv4 must also be considered. Use of IP security at both the IPv4 and IPv6 levels should nevertheless be avoided, for efficiency reasons. If IPv6 is running encrypted, encryption of IPv4 would be redundant except if traffic analysis is felt to be a threat. If IPv6 is running authenticated, authentication of IPv4 will add little. Conversely, IPv4 security will not protect IPv6 traffic once it leaves the IPv6-over-IPv4 domain, so implementing IPv6 security is required even if IPv4 security is available.

There is a possible spoofing attack in which spurious 6over4 packets are injected into a 6over4 domain from outside. Boundary routers MUST discard multicast IPv4 packets with source or destination multicast addresses of organization local scope if they arrive on physical interfaces outside that scope. To defend against spurious unicast 6over4 packets, boundary routers MUST discard incoming IPv4 packets with protocol type 41 from unknown sources: IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels must only be accepted from trusted sources. Unless IPSEC authentication is available, the RECOMMENDED technique is to configure the boundary router only to accept protocol type 41 packets from source addresses within a trusted range or ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the packets are wrapped in IPv4, the usual IPv6 protections do not apply on their own. The edge router has to drop multicast traffic arriving from outside the local scope and accept wrapped packets only from addresses it trusts.
